content: 1. A study compared two types of multiple micronutrient supplements (Sprinkles and Foodlets) with the recommended supplement (Drops) in Iranian infants, as published in Annals of Nutrition and Metabolism in 2009. 2. Research conducted in two rural districts of Indonesia demonstrated that fortifying cooking oil with vitamin A improved the vitamin A status of mothers and children, as reported in 2015. 3. The introduction of red palm oil into a supplementary feeding program in India, distributed through the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS), was evaluated for its impact, as published in the Indian Journal of Public Health in 1999. 4. A study in Ghanaian infants found that a macroand micronutrient-fortified complementary food supplement increased plasma branched-chain amino acid levels, as reported in Annals of Nutrition and Metabolism in 2017. 5. Long-term supplementation with two nutritious food supplements in young children in Niger showed preventive effects, as detailed in the Journal of Nutrition in 2015. 6. A study in North India evaluated the compliance and effects of home-based fortification strategies delivering iron and zinc on hematological and growth markers in children aged 6–24 months, as published in Journal of Health, Population, and Nutrition in 2014. 7. Research on Nias Island, Indonesia, compared locally produced cereal/nut/legume-based biscuits with peanut/milk-based spreads for treating moderately to mildly wasted children, focusing on acceptance and compliance, as reported in the Asia Pacific Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2015. 8. A pilot study in Guinea-Bissau preschools assessed the effectiveness of two ready-to-use supplementary foods (RUSFs) with differing dairy protein content on growth and nutritional status in young children, as published in the FASEB Journal in 2015. 9. A randomized controlled trial in Guinea-Bissau demonstrated that a higher dairy supplement reduced wasting in mothers and had differential impacts on infants and children, depending on maternal supplement response, as reported in Food and Nutrition Bulletin in 2017. 10. A synthesis of three randomized controlled trials in Guinea-Bissau highlighted that higher levels of dairy in supplements improved physical outcomes in children aged 6–59 months, adolescents, and mothers, as published in Food and Nutrition Bulletin in 2018. 11. A study in anemic Cambodian infants aged 6–24 months evaluated the efficacy and safety of twice-weekly administration of iron and folic acid with or without additional micronutrients, as reported in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2009. 12. A randomized controlled trial in rural Bangladesh assessed the variable impact of fortified lipid-based and blended complementary foods on body composition in children, as published in the Journal of Nutrition in 2020. 13. A study in Cambodia evaluated the effects of animal-source foods and micronutrient-fortified complementary foods on body composition, linear growth, and iron status, as part of the WinFood project, as reported in Annals of Nutrition and Metabolism in 2013. 14. A trial in Malawi found that complementary feeding with cowpea reduced growth faltering in rural infants, as published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2017. 15. Including whey protein and whey permeate in ready-to-use supplementary food improved recovery rates in children with moderate acute malnutrition, as demonstrated in a randomized, double-blind clinical trial published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2016. 16. A study in Burkina Faso evaluated the cost-effectiveness of four formulations of food supplements for preventing wasting and stunting, as reported in 2017. 17. A randomized controlled trial in Sierra Leone compared four different supplementary foods for treating moderate acute malnutrition in children, as published in 2018. 18. A study in Cambodia demonstrated that household consumption of thiamin-fortified fish sauce improved erythrocyte thiamin concentrations in women and children under five years of age, as reported in the Journal of Pediatrics in 2016. 19. A randomized controlled trial in Malawi found that extending supplementary feeding for children under five years with moderate acute malnutrition reduced relapse rates, as published in the Journal of Pediatric Gastroenterology and Nutrition in 2015. 20. A study in Vietnam showed that high-energy dense and fortified gruels increased energy and nutrient intakes in infants aged 6–10 months, as reported in Appetite in 2009. 21. A trial in India demonstrated the effectiveness of locally made ready-to-use therapeutic food in managing uncomplicated severe acute malnutrition in a community-based setting, as published in Journal of Tropical Pediatrics in 2013. 22. A study in Argentina evaluated the short-term impact of a food program on the micronutrient nutritional status of children under six years old, as reported in Biological Trace Element Research in 2011. 23. A randomized controlled trial in Cambodia found that exogenous phytase added to small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements improved zinc absorption in young children, as published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in 2019. 24. A study in China assessed the effects of three nutrition interventions on children's growth, hemoglobin concentration, and anemia in poor rural areas, as reported in Annals of Nutrition and Metabolism in 2013. 25. A trial in Jamaica found that early childhood supplementation did not benefit the long-term growth of stunted children, as published in the Journal of Nutrition in 1996.
